questions.problem: In a coffee shop, $28%$ of the customers order their coffee to go. If $12$ customers from the coffee shop are randomly selected, what is the probability that $3$ or less will order their coffee to go? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of customers that order their coffee to go.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=12$ customers

- the probability that each customer orders the coffee to go is $p=28%=0.28$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(12,0.28).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{x}){(0.28)}^{x}{(1-0.28)}^{12-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{x}){(0.28)}^{x}{(0.72)}^{12-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability of getting a "success" (i.e., the customer orders the coffee to go) on at most $3$ trials. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{0}){(0.28)}^{0}{(0.72)}^{12}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{1}){(0.28)}^{1}{(0.72)}^{11}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{2}){(0.28)}^{2}{(0.72)}^{10}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{3}){(0.28)}^{3}{(0.72)}^{9} \\  & ={(0.28)}^{0}{(0.72)}^{12}+12{(0.28)}^{1}{(0.72)}^{11}+66{(0.28)}^{2}{(0.72)}^{10}+220{(0.28)}^{3}{(0.72)}^{9} \\  & =0.555\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem: An archer practices firing an arrow at a target $20$ times. If the archer has a $20%$ chance of hitting the bullseye, what is the probability that the archer hits the bullseye at least $2$ times? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the arrow hits the bullseye. 

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=20$ trials

- the probability of hitting the bull's eye is $p=20%=0.2$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(20,0.2).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{x})(0.2)^{x}(1-0.2)^{20-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{x})(0.2)^{x}(0.8)^{20-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that the archer hits the bullseye at least $2$ times. This corresponds to $P(X\ge 2).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\ge 2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+…+P(X=20)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{0})(0.2)^{0}(0.8)^{20-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{1})(0.2)^{1}(0.8)^{20-1}] \\  & =1-[(0.8)^{20}+20(0.2)(0.8)^{19}] \\  & =1-0.069\,175 \\  & =0.931\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
An unfair coin has a $15%$ chance of landing on heads. The coin is tossed $10$ times. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability of getting heads at least $2$ times?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the coin landed on heads.

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=10$ tosses.

- The probability of landing on heads is $p=15%=0.15.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(10,0.15).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{x})(0.15)^{x}(1-0.15)^{10-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{x})(0.15)^{x}(0.85)^{10-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability of getting heads at least $2$ times. This corresponds to $P(X\ge 2).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\ge 2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+…+P(X=10)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{0})(0.15)^{0}(0.85)^{10-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{1})(0.15)^{1}(0.85)^{10-1}] \\  & =1-[(0.85)^{10}+10(0.15)(0.85)^{9}] \\  & ≈1-0.544\,300 \\  & ≈0.456,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
A fair coin is flipped $4$ times. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability of getting heads exactly $2$ times?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the coin lands on heads.

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=4$ flips.

- The probability of getting heads on a single flip is

$$
p=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(4,\frac{1}{2}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=2$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

Substituting into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=2) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4!}{2!(4-2)!}\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{4} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{16} \\  & =0.375,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
A quality‑check sensor detects a flaw with probability $40%.$ If $5$ items are inspected, rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that at most $2$ of them contain a flaw?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of flawed items detected.

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=5$ items.

- The probability of a flaw is $p=40%=0.4.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(5,0.4).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.4)^{x}(1-0.4)^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.4)^{x}(0.6)^{5-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that at most $2$ of the $5$ items contain flaws. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0})(0.4)^{0}(0.6)^{5}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1})(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{4}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2})(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{3} \\  & =1(0.6)^{5}+5(0.4)(0.6)^{4}+10(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{3} \\  & ≈0.683,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
